title: A city full of thieves
hookLine: the body is a city crowded with lust and anger; meeting the holy, they are broken (Gauri Purbi M4, ang 13)

cards: Lights off. Phone face down. The body exhausted, the mind wide awake.
It replays an argument from lunch. It scrolls through something it wants and can't have. It versions the perfect reply that will never be sent.
The room is quiet, but the city inside is not, and none of the crowd got the memo that it's bedtime. Sohila's fourth hymn is recited at exactly that hour, and it names two of the loudest.

teach.h: FIVE THIEVES THAT STEAL YOUR PEACE.
teach.b: Another hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib names the whole crowd plainly: in this body live five thieves, chor. Kaam, desire out of control. Krodh, anger.
Lobh, greed. Moh, clinging attachment. And hankaar, ego, pride.

That hymn says they plunder the nectar inside; in plain terms, they steal attention, peace, the hours meant for something better. This hymn names the first two, crowding the city. Then it shows the deeper problem.

teach.h: THE THORN OF EGO PRICKS EACH STEP.
teach.b: In paraphrase: the faithless one never tastes the sweetness of God; inside them is the thorn of ego, and the more they walk, the more it pricks.
Anyone with a splinter in their foot knows that picture: you can keep walking, but every step hurts, and the cause is inside. So how is the city cleared? Not by force.
The hymn's answer is humility and company.
In paraphrase: greet the holy with joined palms, a great merit; bow before them, a great merit. Meeting the holy, desire and anger break apart.
And God's humble servants merge in the Name, and the pain of birth and death is broken.

For Sikhs, the holy company is sangat, people gathered to sing God's praise. The hymn doesn't picture anyone fighting the thieves alone in the dark. It pictures joined palms, a bowed head, and good company.
The city clears because better company moves in.

how: Sikhs recite this hymn every night in Kirtan Sohila, and the five thieves (kaam, krodh, lobh, moh, hankaar) are a staple of Sikh teaching, answered by Naam, seva and the sangat.

o: a village where the Gurus once lived
a gate that keeps strangers out at night
a city: here, the body crowded with thieves

games.q: the five thieves — tap the pairs.

s: the Guru Granth Sahib names five thieves living in the body
desire, anger, greed, attachment and pride.
the hymn tells you to fight the thieves alone by willpower
it points to humility and the company of the holy.
in the hymn, the thorn of ego pricks more with every step
the more they walk, the more it pricks.

games.q: your inner city is crowded with desire and anger, and a thorn of ego is in your foot. what does the hymn point you toward?
o: walking faster so you notice the pain less.
joining your palms and meeting the holy company.
leaving the city for the forest.
games.why: greet the holy with joined palms and bow: meeting them, desire and anger are broken apart.

practice: Go slowly through the five, desire, anger, greed, clinging, pride, and quietly name the one that's been loudest this week, without arguing with it.
Picture opening the city gate and letting it walk out, like a guest who stayed too long, and breathe out as it goes. If you pray, join your palms for a moment in the quieter street it leaves.

wordCard.voice: Nagar, a city: Sohila's fourth hymn, the body crowded with desire and anger, the thorn of ego inside, and the holy company that clears the streets.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nagar, a city; in the hymn, the body crowded with desire and anger.

carryVoice: Your line: clear the city. Good company does what force alone can't. Until tomorrow, then.

sources.ref: Gauri Purbi M4, Ang 13 (Kirtan Sohila, hymn 4)
Sorath M3, Ang 600 (the five thieves in the body)
